AmericanFlagSort.stable: No - cycle permutations can reorder equal keys
AmericanFlagSort.inPlace: Yes - elements are permuted in the input
AmericanFlagSort.best: Θ(n) - equal keys need only a range scan
AmericanFlagSort.average: O(n + d × n) - radix levels over the normalized key range
AmericanFlagSort.worst: O(n + d × n) - bounded by the digit count

BPlusTreeSort.stable: Yes (equal keys are inserted to the right of every equal key already present, and splitting preserves key order; see the stability note below)
BPlusTreeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for the nodes)
BPlusTreeSort.best: Θ(n log n) - the tree is built by n insertions regardless of input order
BPlusTreeSort.worst: Θ(n log n) - occupancy bounds the height at log_t((n+1)/2) + 1 for every input

BTreeSort.stable: Yes (equal keys are inserted to the right of every equal key already present, and splitting preserves in-order; see the stability note below)
BTreeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for the nodes)
BTreeSort.best: Θ(n log n) - the tree is built by n insertions regardless of input order
BTreeSort.worst: Θ(n log n) - occupancy bounds the height at log_t((n+1)/2) + 1 for every input

BalancedBinaryTreeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements are inserted to the right, and rotations preserve in-order; see the stability note below)
BalancedBinaryTreeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for tree structure)
BalancedBinaryTreeSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Already sorted or reversed, still requires building balanced tree
BalancedBinaryTreeSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Each of n insertions takes O(log n) comparisons
BalancedBinaryTreeSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by AVL balancing property

BatcherOddEvenMergeSort.stable: No (non-adjacent swaps can change relative order of equal elements)
BatcherOddEvenMergeSort.best: Θ(n log² n) - Data-independent comparison count (same as worst case)
BatcherOddEvenMergeSort.average: Θ(n log² n) - Performs the same comparisons for all inputs
BatcherOddEvenMergeSort.worst: Θ(n log² n) - For n = 2^k: n × log n × (log n − 1) / 4 + n − 1 comparisons

BidirectionalStableQuickSort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of equal elements)
BidirectionalStableQuickSort.inPlace: No (O(n) total auxiliary space across all active recursion levels, O(log n) recursion stack)
BidirectionalStableQuickSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Occurs when pivot consistently divides array into balanced partitions
BidirectionalStableQuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Median-of-3 pivots split near the median on average
BidirectionalStableQuickSort.worst: O(n²) - Occurs when partitioning is maximally unbalanced (probability ~1/n³ with median-of-3)

BinaryInsertSort.stable: Yes (binary search uses <= to preserve order of equal elements)
BinaryInsertSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space, only temp variable for element being inserted)
BinaryInsertSort.best: O(n log n) - Already sorted input moves nothing, but every element is still binary-searched: Σ(i=1 to n-1) ⌊log₂(i+1)⌋ comparisons
BinaryInsertSort.average: O(n²) - Comparisons: O(n log n), Shifts: O(n²) dominate overall complexity
BinaryInsertSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse sorted array, maximum shifts for each element

BinaryTreeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements are inserted to the right, so in-order traversal returns them in insertion order; see the stability note below)
BinaryTreeSort.inPlace: No (Requires O(n) auxiliary space for tree nodes)
BinaryTreeSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Balanced tree (e.g., random input or middle-out insertion)
BinaryTreeSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Tree height is O(log n), each insertion takes O(log n) comparisons
BinaryTreeSort.worst: Θ(n²) - Completely unbalanced tree (e.g., sorted or reverse-sorted input forms a linear chain)

BingoSort.stable: No (a swap that sends a copy of the previous maximum to the end carries the end element back to the scan position, past elements equal to it)
BingoSort.best: Θ(n + m²) - m is the number of distinct keys; reached when the largest keys hold most of the copies, so the region shrinks to about m elements after the first passes; Θ(n) when every key is equal
BingoSort.average: Θ(n·m) - one pass over the unsorted region per distinct key
BingoSort.worst: Θ(n·m) - Θ(n²) when every key is distinct (m = n), where it makes as many passes as selection sort

BinomialHeapSort.stable: No (equal keys are ordered by root-list position, which is degree order rather than insertion order; see the stability note below)
BinomialHeapSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for the node arena)
BinomialHeapSort.best: Θ(n log n) - every extraction pays for the root-list scan and the union, regardless of input order
BinomialHeapSort.worst: Θ(n log n) - the root list never exceeds ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 trees

BitonicRecursiveSort.stable: No (swapping non-adjacent elements can change relative order of equal elements)
BitonicRecursiveSort.inPlace: Yes (no auxiliary buffer; the recursion keeps O(log n) frames on the call stack)
BitonicRecursiveSort.best: Θ(n log² n) - Data-independent comparison count (same as worst case)
BitonicRecursiveSort.average: Θ(n log² n) - Performs the same comparisons for all inputs
BitonicRecursiveSort.worst: Θ(n log² n) - For n = 2^k: n × log n × (log n + 1) / 4 comparisons

BitonicSort.stable: No (swapping non-adjacent elements can change relative order of equal elements)
BitonicSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space - sorts directly on input array)
BitonicSort.best: Θ(n log² n) - Data-independent comparison count (same as worst case)
BitonicSort.average: Θ(n log² n) - Performs the same comparisons for all inputs
BitonicSort.worst: Θ(n log² n) - For n = 2^k: n × log n × (log n + 1) / 4 comparisons

BlockMergeSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space — fixed 512-element cache rented from ArrayPool)
BlockMergeSort.best: O(n) — Already sorted data: all merge-level skips fire

BlockQuickSort.stable: No (partitioning moves elements across equal keys)
BlockQuickSort.inPlace: Yes (an explicit stack of O(log n) ranges and two 128-entry offset buffers)
BlockQuickSort.best: Θ(n log n) - the median of a growing sample splits near the middle; Θ(n) when the duplicate check gathers whole ranges of equal keys
BlockQuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - n log₂ n + o(n log n) comparisons with the median-of-√n pivot
BlockQuickSort.worst: O(n log n) - the depth limit hands a range that keeps splitting badly to heapsort

BottomupHeapSort.stable: No (heap operations do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
BottomupHeapSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space - uses only a few temporary variables)
BottomupHeapSort.best: Ω(n log n) - every sift descends to a leaf, even when all keys are equal
BottomupHeapSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Build heap O(n) + n-1 deletions of log n + O(1) comparisons each
BottomupHeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - at most 1.5n log n + O(n) comparisons (Wegener)

BottomupMergeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements maintain relative order via <= comparison during merge)
BottomupMergeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for merging)
BottomupMergeSort.best: O(n log n) - Even sorted data requires ⌈log₂(n)⌉ passes of merging (this implementation skips the comparisons of a merge already in order, but each pass still copies all n elements; see the implementation note)
BottomupMergeSort.average: O(n log n) - ⌈log₂(n)⌉ passes with n work per pass
BottomupMergeSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed performance regardless of input

BubbleSort.stable: Yes (equal elements are never swapped due to strict comparison)
BubbleSort.best: O(n) - With early termination optimization, sorted input only requires one pass
BubbleSort.average: O(n²) - Expected n(n-1)/4 swaps for random input
BubbleSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse-sorted input requires n(n-1)/2 swaps

BucketSort.inPlace: No (O(n + k) auxiliary space for buckets)
BucketSort.best: Ω(n + k) - Uniform distribution, each bucket has ~n/k elements
BucketSort.average: Θ(n + k) - Assumes uniform distribution: the buckets cost Θ(n + n²/k + k) in expectation, which is Θ(n) for k = Θ(n)
BucketSort.worst: O(n²) - All elements in one bucket, degenerates to Insertion Sort

BucketSortInteger.inPlace: No (O(n + k) auxiliary space for buckets)
BucketSortInteger.best: Ω(n + k) - Uniform distribution, each bucket has ~n/k elements
BucketSortInteger.average: Θ(n + k) - Assumes uniform distribution: the buckets cost Θ(n + n²/k + k) in expectation, which is Θ(n) for k = Θ(n)
BucketSortInteger.worst: O(n²) - All elements in one bucket, degenerates to Insertion Sort

CartesianTreeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for tree nodes and O(n) for the stack / priority queue)
CartesianTreeSort.best: Θ(n) - the Cartesian tree is a path (sorted or reverse-sorted input), so the priority queue never holds more than one node
CartesianTreeSort.worst: Θ(n log n) - construction is always linear; extraction is bounded by n extract-min operations on a queue of at most n nodes

CircleSort.stable: No (long-distance swaps do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
CircleSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) stack space for recursion)
CircleSort.best: O(n log n) - Sorted input still requires one full pass

CocktailShakerSort.stable: Yes (equal elements never swapped due to strict comparison)
CocktailShakerSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted, only one forward pass with n-1 comparisons
CocktailShakerSort.average: O(n²) - Expected n(n-1)/4 swaps for random input
CocktailShakerSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse-sorted input requires n(n-1)/2 comparisons and swaps

CombSort.stable: No (long-distance swaps do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
CombSort.best: Ω(n log n) - Already sorted, but all gap passes must still be performed
CombSort.average: Θ(n²/2^p) where p is the number of increments - Empirically O(n log n) with shrink factor 1.3
CombSort.worst: O(n²) - Certain input patterns can degrade to quadratic time

CountingSort.inPlace: No (O(n + k) where k = range of keys)
CountingSort.best: O(n + k) - Every input does the same work; no pattern is favourable
CountingSort.average: O(n + k) - Linear in input size plus key range
CountingSort.worst: O(n + k) - Independent of how the keys are distributed

CountingSortInteger.inPlace: No (O(n + k) where k = range of values)
CountingSortInteger.best: O(n + k) - Every input does the same work; no pattern is favourable
CountingSortInteger.average: O(n + k) - Linear in input size plus value range
CountingSortInteger.worst: O(n + k) - Independent of how the values are distributed

CycleSort.family: Selection (though often classified separately due to unique cycle-based approach)
CycleSort.stable: No (relative order of equal elements is not preserved)
CycleSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space, only constant extra variables)
CycleSort.best: Θ(n²) - sorted input still counts once from every start position: n(n-1)/2 comparisons and no writes
CycleSort.average: Θ(n²) - every placed element costs another count over the range after its cycle's start
CycleSort.worst: Θ(n²) - about 3n²/2 comparisons when one cycle runs through every element; at most n writes

DestswapStableQuickSort.stable: Yes (stable 2-way partition and order-preserving buffer roles keep equal elements in original relative order)
DestswapStableQuickSort.inPlace: No (O(n) pooled scratch buffer, O(log n) recursion stack)
DestswapStableQuickSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Occurs when pivot consistently divides array into balanced partitions; Θ(n) when all elements are equal
DestswapStableQuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - the pseudo-median splits near the median
DestswapStableQuickSort.worst: O(n²) - pivots that keep splitting off a constant number of elements

DoubleSelectionSort.stable: No (swapping non-adjacent elements can change relative order of equal elements)
DoubleSelectionSort.best: Θ(n²) - the comparisons do not depend on the input; sorted input swaps nothing
DoubleSelectionSort.average: Θ(n²) - about 3n²/8 comparisons, a quarter fewer than selection sort's n²/2
DoubleSelectionSort.worst: Θ(n²) - the same comparisons; at most two swaps per pass

Driftsort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of equal elements)
Driftsort.inPlace: No (auxiliary buffer of about n elements; n/2 for very large inputs)
Driftsort.best: O(n) - Fully ascending or descending input sorts with exactly n-1 comparisons
Driftsort.average: O(n log k) where k is the number of distinct values - Equal-partition trick exploits duplicates
Driftsort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by the powersort merge tree and the bounded quicksort recursion

DropMergeSort.family: Merge (the longest nondecreasing subsequence and the sorted dropped elements are merged)
DropMergeSort.stable: No (relative order of equal elements is not preserved)
DropMergeSort.inPlace: No (O(K) auxiliary space where K is the number of out-of-order elements)
DropMergeSort.best: O(N) - When data is already sorted or nearly sorted (K ≈ 0), only LNS extraction and merge are needed
DropMergeSort.average: O(N + K log K) - Expected when K < 0.2N with K elements randomly distributed
DropMergeSort.worst: O(N log N) - Falls back to QuickSort when disorder exceeds 60% (early-out), or when K ≈ N

DualPivotQuickSort.stable: No (partitioning does not preserve relative order of equal elements)
DualPivotQuickSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack)
DualPivotQuickSort.best: Θ(n) - all elements equal: the pivots are equal, the center is never sorted, and the outer parts are empty
DualPivotQuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - 1.9 n ln n ≈ 1.32 n log₂ n comparisons on random distinct keys (Wild and Nebel)
DualPivotQuickSort.worst: O(n²) - pivots that keep splitting off a constant number of elements

FlashSort.stable: No (permutation phase does not preserve relative order)
FlashSort.inPlace: Yes (O(m) auxiliary space for class boundaries only)
FlashSort.best: Ω(n) - Uniform distribution, one pass over the array
FlashSort.average: Θ(n) - Assumes uniform distribution, permutation phase is O(n)
FlashSort.worst: O(n²) - All elements in one class, degenerates to Insertion Sort

FlatStableSort.stable: Yes (≤ comparison in all merge operations preserves relative order)
FlatStableSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n / BLOCK_SIZE) block-index storage plus O(BLOCK_SIZE) circular scratch)
FlatStableSort.best: Θ(n) - an already ordered input of more than 7 blocks is settled by one scan, the figure Boost states for flat_stable_sort
FlatStableSort.worst: O(n log n) (balanced binary split at block granularity)

FluxSort.stable: Yes (both partition destinations are filled in scan order, equal elements stay on the not-greater side, and quadsort is stable)
FluxSort.inPlace: No (n elements of swap memory shared with quadsort, which also hold the pivot stack)
FluxSort.best: Θ(n) - ordered input is recognised by the analysis with about n comparisons, strictly descending input is reversed, and low-cardinality ranges collapse by reverse partitions
FluxSort.average: Θ(n log n) - the sampled pivot splits each range near its median
FluxSort.worst: O(n log n) - a partition continues only on a split no worse than 1:32; otherwise the larger side goes to quadsort, or, when the greater side is the small one, a reverse partition removes the pivot's duplicates (at least 1/17 of the range) before partitioning continues, or hands the rest to quadsort

Glidesort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of equal elements)
Glidesort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space by default, degrades gracefully with less)
Glidesort.best: O(n) - Already sorted or reverse sorted data (single run detected)
Glidesort.average: O(n log k) where k is the number of distinct values - Exploits duplicates via quicksort partitioning
Glidesort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by powersort merge tree and bounded quicksort recursion

GnomeSort.stable: Yes (strict inequality preserves relative order of equal elements)
GnomeSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted, only n-1 comparisons needed
GnomeSort.average: O(n²) - Approximately n²/4 comparisons and swaps
GnomeSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse sorted, exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons and n(n-1)/2 swaps

HeapSort.stable: No (heap operations do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
HeapSort.best: Θ(n) - when all keys are equal, every sift stops at its first level; with distinct keys the best case is Θ(n log n)
HeapSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Build heap O(n) + n-1 extractions with O(log n) heapify each
HeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed upper bound regardless of input distribution

InsertionSort.stable: Yes (strict inequality > preserves order of equal elements)
InsertionSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space, only temp variable for element being inserted)
InsertionSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted array, only n-1 comparisons, zero writes
InsertionSort.average: O(n²) - On average, each element shifts halfway back (n²/4 comparisons and writes)
InsertionSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse sorted array, maximum shifts: n(n-1)/2 comparisons and writes

IntroSort.stable: No (partitioning and heapsort exchange elements across equal keys)
IntroSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) recursion depth, bounded by the depth limit)
IntroSort.best: Θ(n log n) - every range above the threshold is partitioned; sorted input splits evenly at every level
IntroSort.average: Θ(n log n) - median-of-3 pivots split near the median on average
IntroSort.worst: O(n log n) - the depth limit hands a range that keeps splitting badly to heapsort

IntroSortDotnet.stable: No (QuickSort and HeapSort are unstable; element order is not preserved for equal values)
IntroSortDotnet.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack, no additional arrays allocated)
IntroSortDotnet.best: Θ(n log n) - Occurs when QuickSort consistently creates balanced partitions and InsertionSort handles small subarrays efficiently
IntroSortDotnet.average: Θ(n log n) - median-of-3 pivots split near the median on average
IntroSortDotnet.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by HeapSort fallback when recursion depth exceeds 2(⌊log₂(n)⌋ + 1)

Ipnsort.inPlace: Yes for large elements; small-sort scratch of at most 48 pooled elements otherwise (the reference uses a stack array, unavailable for generic T in C#)
Ipnsort.best: Θ(n) - A non-descending or strictly descending input longer than 20 elements is recognised as one run with n-1 comparisons (and reversed if descending)
Ipnsort.average: Θ(n log n); O(n log k) for k distinct values - the equal-partition step removes a run of keys equal to an ancestor pivot
Ipnsort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by the bounded partition count plus heapsort fallback

LibrarySort.stable: Yes - upper-bound insertion and ordered redistribution
LibrarySort.inPlace: No - gapped element storage and dense staging
LibrarySort.best: Θ(n log n) - binary searches with short shifts
LibrarySort.average: O(n log n) - random arrival order
LibrarySort.worst: O(n²) - clustered insertions can require long shifts

MergeInsertionSort.stable: No (the Jacobsthal insertion order can place a later equal key before an earlier one)
MergeInsertionSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for pended elements and indices)
MergeInsertionSort.best: O(n log n) - Optimal comparison count, approaches ceiling(log₂(n!)) comparisons
MergeInsertionSort.average: O(n log n) - Comparisons remain near-optimal, but data movement is O(n²)
MergeInsertionSort.worst: O(n²) - Due to insertion shifts, though comparison count remains O(n log n)

MergeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements maintain relative order via <= comparison during merge)
MergeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for merging)
MergeSort.best: O(n log n) - Merge sort as defined runs every merge, so even sorted data goes through ⌈log₂(n)⌉ levels of merging (this implementation skips them; see the implementation note)
MergeSort.average: O(n log n) - Balanced recursion tree with n work per level
MergeSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed balanced partitioning regardless of input

MinHeapSort.stable: No (heap operations do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
MinHeapSort.best: Θ(n) - when all keys are equal, every sift stops at its first level; with distinct keys the best case is Θ(n log n)
MinHeapSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Build heap O(n) + n-1 extractions with O(log n) heapify each + O(n) reversal
MinHeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed upper bound regardless of input distribution

NaturalMergeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements maintain relative order: the left run's element is placed first)
NaturalMergeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for merging)
NaturalMergeSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted or fully reversed data is a single run; only one detection scan needed
NaturalMergeSort.average: O(n log n) - Random data has ~n/2 runs, requiring ~log₂(n) merge passes
NaturalMergeSort.worst: O(n log n) - Alternating up/down data produces many small runs, requiring full merge passes

OddEvenSort.stable: Yes (only swaps strictly out-of-order elements, preserving relative order of equal elements)
OddEvenSort.best: Ω(n) - Already sorted, one pass (both phases) with n-1 comparisons and no swaps
OddEvenSort.average: Θ(n²) - Approximately n/2 to n passes, each with ~n/2 comparisons, totaling ~n²/2 comparisons
OddEvenSort.worst: O(n²) - Reversed array requires ~n passes, each with ~n/2 comparisons, totaling ~n²/2 comparisons

PDQSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack)
PDQSort.best: Θ(n) - Sorted, reverse sorted, all equal elements (pattern detection + partial insertion sort)
PDQSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Median-of-3 and ninther pivots split near the median on average
PDQSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by HeapSort fallback when the bad partition limit is reached

PDQSortBranchless.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) stack + 128 bytes of offset buffers per partition call)
PDQSortBranchless.best: Θ(n) - Sorted, reverse sorted, all equal elements

PairInsertionSort.stable: Yes (the later element of a tied pair is inserted above the earlier one, and no scan passes an equal key)
PairInsertionSort.best: O(n) - sorted input costs three comparisons per pair and moves nothing
PairInsertionSort.average: O(n²) - about n²/6 comparisons and writes on random input, against n²/4 for straight insertion
PairInsertionSort.worst: O(n²) - reverse-sorted input: the larger element of each pair passes the whole prefix, about n²/4 comparisons and writes

PairingHeapSort.stable: No (equal keys are ordered by child-list position, which the pairing passes reorder; see the stability note below)
PairingHeapSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for the node arena)
PairingHeapSort.best: Θ(n) - a descending run makes every insert the new root, leaving a chain whose every extraction has a single child to pair
PairingHeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - extraction is O(log n) amortized; a single extraction may cost O(n)

PairwiseSortingNetwork.stable: No (pair layers past the first compare non-adjacent positions: [1a, 1b, 0] ends as [0, 1b, 1a])
PairwiseSortingNetwork.best: Θ(n log² n) - Data-independent comparison count (same as worst case)
PairwiseSortingNetwork.average: Θ(n log² n) - Performs the same comparisons for all inputs
PairwiseSortingNetwork.worst: Θ(n log² n) - For n = 2^k: n × log n × (log n − 1) / 4 + n − 1 comparisons

PancakeSort.family: Selection (selects maximum and places it in correct position)
PancakeSort.stable: No (flipping changes relative order of equal elements)
PancakeSort.best: Θ(n²) - Already sorted, still must find maximum in each iteration (no flips needed)
PancakeSort.average: Θ(n²) - Comparisons are always n(n-1)/2; close to 2n flips, since the maximum ends its prefix only by chance
PancakeSort.worst: Θ(n²) - At most 2n - 3 flips; each pass flips at most the whole remaining prefix

PatienceSort.family: Merge (piles are dealt by binary search, then combined by a k-way merge)
PatienceSort.stable: No (relative order of equal elements may not be preserved)
PatienceSort.best: O(n) - Reverse-sorted (non-increasing) input produces 1 pile; merge is trivial
PatienceSort.average: Θ(n log k) - where k is the average LIS length
PatienceSort.worst: O(n log n) - Already sorted (ascending) input produces n piles

PigeonSort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of elements with equal keys)
PigeonSort.inPlace: No (O(n + k) auxiliary space where k = range of keys)
PigeonSort.best: O(n + k) - All cases have the same complexity
PigeonSort.average: O(n + k) - Linear in input size plus key range
PigeonSort.worst: O(n + k) - Even with all elements having different keys

PigeonSortInteger.stable: Yes, vacuously — equal integers are indistinguishable, so no relative order is observable
PigeonSortInteger.inPlace: No (O(k) where k = range of values; independent of n)
PigeonSortInteger.best: O(n + k) - All cases have the same complexity
PigeonSortInteger.average: O(n + k) - Linear in input size plus value range
PigeonSortInteger.worst: O(n + k) - Even with all elements having different values

PingpongMergeSort.stable: Yes (equal elements maintain relative order via <= comparison during merge)
PingpongMergeSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space — one full-size buffer)
PingpongMergeSort.best: O(n log n) writes, O(n) comparisons — sorted data skips merges but still propagates through levels
PingpongMergeSort.average: O(n log n) — balanced recursion tree with n writes per level
PingpongMergeSort.worst: O(n log n) — guaranteed balanced partitioning regardless of input

PoplarHeapSort.stable: No (sift and root exchanges move equal keys past each other)
PoplarHeapSort.best: Ω(n log n) - building a sorted input is linear, but every extraction still walks the O(log n) poplar roots

PowerSort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of equal elements)
PowerSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n/2) temporary space for merging)
PowerSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted or reverse sorted data (single run)
PowerSort.average: O(n log n) - Optimal merge tree construction
PowerSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by power-based merge strategy

QuadSort.stable: Yes (every merge takes the left element on ties, and only strictly descending stretches are reversed)
QuadSort.inPlace: No (n elements of swap memory, plus the 32-element stack array)
QuadSort.best: Θ(n) - ordered or strictly descending input is recognised by the quad swap with about n comparisons; descending input is then reversed
QuadSort.average: Θ(n log n) - each quad merge level halves the number of runs twice
QuadSort.worst: O(n log n) - the swap memory holds more than n / 8 elements, so the rotate merge levels recurse a bounded number of times before their pieces fit

QuickSort.stable: No (partitioning does not preserve relative order of equal elements)
QuickSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for explicit stack, guaranteed by smaller-partition-first strategy)
QuickSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Balanced partitions (pivot divides array into two equal halves)
QuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Expected number of comparisons: 2n ln n ≈ 1.39n log₂ n
QuickSort.worst: O(n²) - Occurs when pivot is always the smallest or largest element (e.g., sorted or reverse-sorted arrays with poor pivot selection)

QuickSortMedian3.stable: No (partitioning does not preserve relative order of equal elements)
QuickSortMedian3.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack, O(1) for partitioning)
QuickSortMedian3.best: Θ(n log n) - Sorted input partitions perfectly with zero effective swaps
QuickSortMedian3.average: Θ(n log n) - Expected (12/7) n ln n ≈ 1.19 n log₂ n comparisons on distinct keys (Sedgewick)
QuickSortMedian3.worst: O(n²) - Occurs when partitioning is maximally unbalanced (probability ~1/n³ with median-of-3)

QuickSortMedian9.stable: No (partitioning does not preserve relative order of equal elements)
QuickSortMedian9.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack, O(1) for partitioning)
QuickSortMedian9.best: Θ(n log n) - Sorted input partitions perfectly with zero effective swaps
QuickSortMedian9.average: Θ(n log n) - Tukey's ninther lowers the leading constant below median-of-3's (12/7) n ln n ≈ 1.19 n log₂ n
QuickSortMedian9.worst: O(n²) - Occurs when partitioning is maximally unbalanced (probability < 1/n⁹, extremely unlikely)

RadixLSD10Sort.inPlace: No (O(n) auxiliary space for the temporary buffer, plus d × 11 stack counters)
RadixLSD10Sort.best: Θ(n) - When all elements are identical (early termination on range == 0)
RadixLSD10Sort.average: Θ(d × n) - Linear in input size, independent of value distribution
RadixLSD10Sort.worst: Θ(d × n) - Performance depends on digit count, not comparisons

RadixLSD256Sort.stable: Yes (maintains relative order of elements with equal keys)
RadixLSD256Sort.inPlace: No (O(n) auxiliary space for temporary buffer)
RadixLSD256Sort.best: Θ(n) - When all elements are identical (early termination on range == 0)
RadixLSD256Sort.average: Θ(d × n) - Linear in input size, where d depends on actual value range
RadixLSD256Sort.worst: Θ(d × n) - Same complexity regardless of input order, d = ⌈keyBits/8⌉ for full range

RadixLSD4Sort.stable: Yes (maintains relative order of elements with equal keys)
RadixLSD4Sort.inPlace: No (O(n) auxiliary space for temporary buffer)
RadixLSD4Sort.best: Θ(n) - When all elements are identical (early termination on range == 0)
RadixLSD4Sort.average: Θ(d × n) - Linear in input size, where d depends on actual key range
RadixLSD4Sort.worst: Θ(d × n) - Same complexity regardless of input order, d = ⌈keyBits/2⌉ for full range

RadixMSD10Sort.best: Θ(n) - equal keys need only a range scan
RadixMSD10Sort.average: O(n + d × n) - radix levels over the normalized key range
RadixMSD10Sort.worst: O(n + d × n) - bounded by the digit count

RadixMSD4Sort.best: Θ(n) - equal keys need only a range scan
RadixMSD4Sort.average: O(n + d × n) - radix levels over the normalized key range
RadixMSD4Sort.worst: O(n + d × n) - bounded by the digit count

Radsort.family: Distribution (Radix Sort, LSD variant; each digit is distributed into chains of fixed-size blocks that reuse consumed input blocks)
Radsort.stable: Yes (input blocks are read in logical order, a bucket's blocks are drawn at increasing logical indices, and the fixup keeps that order)
Radsort.inPlace: No (O(√n) auxiliary space: 2σ scratch blocks of b elements plus per-block bookkeeping, with b ∈ Θ(√n))
Radsort.best: Θ(n) - all keys equal: the range scan finds range 0 and no pass runs. With a non-zero range, Θ(d × n): every pass moves every element whatever the order
Radsort.average: Θ(d × n) - each pass reads and writes every element once; the fixup touches O(n/b) block entries and moves no element
Radsort.worst: Θ(d × n) - the same work regardless of input order

RotateLSDRadixSort.family: Distribution (Radix Sort, LSD variant; each digit is sorted by an in-place rotation merge sort)
RotateLSDRadixSort.stable: Yes (every merge puts the left run's block before the right run's block in each digit group, and rotations keep the order inside a block)
RotateLSDRadixSort.inPlace: Yes (no auxiliary element buffer; only the recursion stack)
RotateLSDRadixSort.best: Θ(n) - all keys equal: the range scan finds range 0 and no pass runs. With a non-zero range, Θ(d × n) when every pass finds its digit already in order: each binary search lands on the run boundary and no rotation moves anything
RotateLSDRadixSort.average: Θ(d × n log n) - each pass is a merge sort whose merges rotate a constant fraction of their elements
RotateLSDRadixSort.worst: O(d × n log n) - a merge of L elements rotates at most L elements on each level of the digit bisection, and radix 4 bisects twice

RotateMergeSort.inPlace: Yes (no external buffer; merge uses O(log n) explicit stack via stackalloc)
RotateMergeSort.best: O(n) – Sorted data: insertion sort is linear on each block, and in the rotate merge every binary search lands on the run boundary, so no rotation moves anything and a merge of two runs of length m ends after O(log² m) comparisons; summed over the passes that is O(n) (this implementation skips those merges outright; see the implementation note)
RotateMergeSort.average: O(n log² n) – Binary search (log n) + rotation (n) per merge × log n passes

RotateMergeSortRecursive.inPlace: Yes (no external buffer, uses rotation for in-place merging)
RotateMergeSortRecursive.best: O(n) - Sorted data: insertion sort is linear on each small partition, and in the rotate merge every binary search lands on the run boundary, so no rotation moves anything and a merge of two halves of length m ends after O(log² m) comparisons; T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(log² n) is O(n) (this implementation skips those merges outright; see the implementation note)
RotateMergeSortRecursive.average: O(n log² n) - Binary search (log n) + rotation (n) per merge level (log n levels)
RotateMergeSortRecursive.worst: O(n log² n) - Rotation adds O(n) factor to each merge operation

SampleSort.stable: No (partitioning exchanges elements across the range, and the sample draw moves elements to the front)
SampleSort.inPlace: Yes (the sample is kept inside the range being sorted; O(log n) explicit stack)
SampleSort.best: Θ(n log n) - every element is compared with the pivots on its path, Θ(log n) of them even when the sample splits evenly
SampleSort.average: Θ(n log n) - expected comparisons n log₂ n (1 + o(1)), approaching log₂ n! as the sample grows with n
SampleSort.worst: O(n log³ n) - every draw takes the extremes of its range, so all non-sample elements land in one subarray; even then each round fixes its whole sample of about n / ln n elements, so W(n) ≤ W(sample) + O(n log n) + W(n − sample). A sample that does not grow with n would leave QuickSort's O(n²)

SelectionSort.stable: No (swapping non-adjacent elements can change relative order of equal elements)
SelectionSort.best: Θ(n²) - Always performs n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of input order
SelectionSort.average: Θ(n²) - Same comparison count; swap count varies but doesn't dominate
SelectionSort.worst: Θ(n²) - Same comparison count; at most n-1 swaps

ShellSortCiura2001.stable: No - gap passes may reorder equal keys

ShellSortKnuth1973.stable: No - gap passes may reorder equal keys

ShellSortLee2021.stable: No - gap passes may reorder equal keys

ShellSortSedgewick1986.stable: No - gap passes may reorder equal keys

ShellSortTokuda1992.stable: No - gap passes may reorder equal keys

ShiftSort.family: Merge (adaptive, divide and conquer over a derivative list)
ShiftSort.stable: Yes (the three-element swap only reorders a strictly descending window, and merges break ties toward the left sublist)
ShiftSort.inPlace: No (requires the derivative list and a merge list alongside the input)
ShiftSort.best: O(n) - an empty derivative list means the array is already sorted, so the scan is all the work
ShiftSort.average: O(n log n) - the same order as merge sort; a shorter derivative list only lowers the constant
ShiftSort.worst: O(n log n) - a reverse-sorted array, whose descending windows yield the maximum ⌈n/2⌉ sublists

SmoothSort.stable: No (heap operations do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
SmoothSort.inPlace: Yes (O(1) auxiliary space - only uses variables for heap size tracking)
SmoothSort.best: Ω(n) - Already sorted data requires only O(n) comparisons during heap construction with no swaps
SmoothSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Typical random data requires O(n log n) comparisons and element moves
SmoothSort.worst: O(n log n) - every sift and trinkle is bounded by the depth of the Leonardo trees, about log_φ n

SpinSort.stable: Yes (≤ comparison in all merge operations preserves relative order)
SpinSort.inPlace: No (requires O(ceil(n/2)) temporary space for the half buffer)
SpinSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted or strictly descending data (a sorted prefix with a short unsorted tail costs O(n + t log t) for a tail of t elements)
SpinSort.average: O(n log n) - Balanced recursive merge
SpinSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by balanced binary split

SplaySort.stable: Yes (equal elements go right during BST insertion; BST rotations preserve in-order traversal, so insertion order is maintained)
SplaySort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for tree nodes with parent pointers)
SplaySort.best: Θ(n) - reached when each element is adjacent in sorted order to the one inserted before it, which holds for both sorted and reverse-sorted input (see Adaptive Behavior)
SplaySort.average: Θ(n log n) amortized - guaranteed by splay tree amortized analysis
SplaySort.worst: O(n log n) - the splay tree's amortized bound applied to a sequence of n insertions; a single insertion may still cost Θ(n)

SpreadSort.stable: No (the in-place redistribution moves each element directly to its bin, which does not preserve relative order)
SpreadSort.inPlace: Partially (distribution is in-place, but this implementation uses an auxiliary bin cache).
SpreadSort.best: O(n) - When data is already sorted (early detection)
SpreadSort.average: O(n √(log n)) - Hybrid distribution and comparison
SpreadSort.worst: O(n * (K/S + S)) where K = log₂(range), S = max_splits

StableQuickSort.stable: Yes (preserves relative order of equal elements)
StableQuickSort.inPlace: No (O(n) total auxiliary space across all active recursion levels, O(log n) recursion stack)
StableQuickSort.best: Θ(n log n) - Occurs when pivot consistently divides array into balanced partitions
StableQuickSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Median-of-3 pivots split near the median on average
StableQuickSort.worst: O(n²) - Occurs when partitioning is maximally unbalanced (probability ~1/n³ with median-of-3)

StdSort.inPlace: Yes (O(log n) recursion stack, no additional arrays allocated)
StdSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted with partition detection
StdSort.average: O(n log n) - Typical random data
StdSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by HeapSort fallback

StrandSort.family: Merge (each extracted strand is merged into the accumulated result)
StrandSort.stable: Yes (a strand takes equal elements in input order, and the merge prefers the accumulated result on ties, so an element never passes one extracted before it)
StrandSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted input produces one strand; merge is trivial
StrandSort.average: O(n√n) - Random input typically produces O(√n) strands
StrandSort.worst: O(n²) - Reverse-sorted input produces n strands of length 1

SymMergeSort.stable: Yes (≥ comparison in binary search preserves relative order)
SymMergeSort.inPlace: Yes (no external buffer; the symmetric recursion needs an O(log n) stack)
SymMergeSort.best: O(n) – Sorted data: insertion sort is linear on each block, and each pair's symmetric binary search ends at the run boundary, so nothing is rotated and the merge stops after that one search; a pass over runs of width w costs O((n/w)·log w) comparisons, which shrinks geometrically from pass to pass, so the passes sum to O(n) (this implementation skips those merges outright; see the implementation note)
SymMergeSort.average: O(n log² n) moves, O(n log n) comparisons
SymMergeSort.worst: O(n log² n) moves, O(n log n) comparisons

TernaryHeapSort.stable: No (heap operations do not preserve relative order of equal elements)
TernaryHeapSort.best: Θ(n) - when all keys are equal, every sift stops at its first level; with distinct keys the best case is Θ(n log n)
TernaryHeapSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Build heap O(n) + n-1 extractions with O(log₃ n) heapify each
TernaryHeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed upper bound regardless of input distribution

TimSort.stable: Yes (≤ comparison in ascending run detection and merging preserves relative order)
TimSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n/2) temporary space worst-case for merging)
TimSort.best: O(n) - Already sorted or reverse sorted data (single run detected, n-1 comparisons)
TimSort.average: O(n log n) - Balanced run detection and merge tree with adaptive behavior
TimSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed by minRun calculation (ensures balanced merges) and stack invariants (ensures O(log n) depth)

TournamentSort.stable: Yes (a tie goes to the left contestant, which holds the earlier element)
TournamentSort.inPlace: No (O(n) output area in addition to the O(n) winner tree)
TournamentSort.best: Θ(n log n) - every extraction replays a leaf-to-root path

TreapSort.stable: Yes (equal elements are inserted to the right, and rotations preserve in-order regardless of the priorities; see the stability note below)
TreapSort.inPlace: No (requires O(n) auxiliary space for tree nodes with parent pointers and priorities)
TreapSort.average: Θ(n log n) expected - guaranteed by random priority assignment
TreapSort.worst: O(n²) with astronomically low probability (when random priorities produce degenerate tree)

WeakHeapSort.stable: No (element order changes arbitrarily during heap operations)
WeakHeapSort.inPlace: Nearly (requires O(n) bits for reverse array ≈ n/64 ulongs = n/8 bytes overhead)
WeakHeapSort.best: Ω(n log n) - every extraction merges the root with each node of the distinguished path, whatever the input
WeakHeapSort.average: Θ(n log n) - Build weak heap O(n) + extract phase O(n log n)
WeakHeapSort.worst: O(n log n) - Guaranteed upper bound for all inputs
